passages.t: ‘His loving devotion endures forever’, and ‘What can man do to me?’
passages.happening:
Psalm 118 closes the Hallel, the six psalms of praise sung at the feasts. It opens and closes with the same line. “Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His loving devotion endures forever” (verse 1). Then three groups are called to answer. “Let Israel say, ‘His loving devotion endures forever’” (verse 2). The house of Aaron and those who fear the LORD say it too (verses 3 and 4).

Then one person tells his story. “In my distress I called to the LORD, and He answered and set me free” (verse 5). “The LORD is on my side; I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?” (verse 6). He draws a lesson. “It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in man” (verse 8). “It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in princes” (verse 9).

He was in great danger. “All the nations surrounded me” (verse 10). “They swarmed around me like bees, but they were extinguished like burning thorns” (verse 12). Three times he says, “in the name of the LORD I cut them off” (verses 10 to 12). “I was pushed so hard I was falling, but the LORD helped me” (verse 13). “The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The opening sounds like worship with many voices. A leader calls, and the people answer with the same refrain. Psalm 115 did the same with the same three groups: Israel, the priests, and those who fear the LORD.

Who is the ‘I’ who was surrounded? Many scholars think he was first a king, coming back from war to give thanks at the temple. Others think he speaks for the whole people, perhaps after the exile, when Israel was small and surrounded by enemies. The psalm can be read both ways.

Verse 14 is a quotation. It is word for word the line Moses and Israel sang after crossing the sea: “The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation” (Exodus 15:2). So the singer sets his own rescue beside the exodus. God has done it again.

Bees swarm fast, and thorns burn hot and quickly die. The enemies were fierce, but they did not last.
passages.later:
Hebrews quotes verse 6 to steady believers: “So we say with confidence: ‘The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?’” (Hebrews 13:6).

Isaiah repeats verse 14 in his own song of praise: “For the LORD GOD is my strength and my song, and He also has become my salvation” (Isaiah 12:2).
passages.hard: What about ‘in the name of the LORD I cut them off’? These lines describe a fight for survival: the singer is surrounded and falling, and he gives the victory to God. They are not a call to attack anyone, and they name no people of today. The New Testament reads this psalm through Jesus, who won his victory by being rejected and raised, not by killing enemies. Paul tells believers, “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:21).
passages.asks:
‘What can man do to me?’ is a brave question. It does not mean nothing bad can happen. It means that people do not have the last word over someone God holds.

Where are you putting your trust: in people with power, or in the LORD? Verses 8 and 9 do not say people are worthless. They say there is a better place to take refuge.

passages.t: ‘I will not die, but I will live’, and ‘Open to me the gates of righteousness’
passages.happening:
Now there is joy. “Shouts of joy and salvation resound in the tents of the righteous: ‘The right hand of the LORD performs with valor!’” (verse 15).

The rescued man sings, “I will not die, but I will live and proclaim what the LORD has done” (verse 17). He admits his trouble was hard. “The LORD disciplined me severely, but He has not given me over to death” (verse 18).

Then he reaches the temple. “Open to me the gates of righteousness, that I may enter and give thanks to the LORD” (verse 19). An answer comes from inside. “This is the gate of the LORD; the righteous shall enter through it” (verse 20). He goes in. “I will give You thanks, for You have answered me, and You have become my salvation” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
These verses sound like a procession arriving at the temple. The man outside asks for the gates to open, and someone at the gate answers. Psalms 15 and 24 have the same kind of exchange at the gate: who may come in?

‘The right hand of the LORD’ is said three times in verses 15 and 16. The right hand was the strong hand, the hand of power in battle.

Verse 18 is honest. The rescued man does not say he never suffered. He says God disciplined him hard, and yet did not give him over to death. He holds both together.
passages.later:
Jesus said, “I am the gate. If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved” (John 10:9).

Hebrews says that God disciplines those he loves, and that discipline is a sign of being his children (Hebrews 12:6-7).
passages.asks:
‘I will not die, but I will live and proclaim what the LORD has done.’ The purpose of the rescued life is to tell what God did. If you have been brought through something, who needs to hear it?

Verse 18 also helps when life has been hard. A believer may say both that God has been severe and that God has been good. Psalm 118 says both.

passages.t: ‘The stone the builders rejected’, ‘This is the day’, and ‘Blessed is he who comes’
passages.happening:
Now come the best-known lines of the psalm. “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. This is from the LORD, and it is marvelous in our eyes” (verses 22 and 23). “This is the day that the LORD has made; we will rejoice and be glad in it” (verse 24).

Then the people pray. “O LORD, save us, we pray. We beseech You, O LORD, cause us to prosper!” (verse 25). And a blessing comes from the temple. “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD. From the house of the LORD we bless you” (verse 26).

There is light, and a sacrifice at the altar (verse 27). The singer says, “You are my God, and I will give You thanks” (verse 28). The psalm ends where it began. “Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His loving devotion endures forever” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
The cornerstone was the most important stone in a building. It may have been the large stone at the base that set the line of the walls, or the stone at the top that held an arch together. Readers take it both ways. Either way, the picture is plain: builders looked at a stone and threw it aside as useless. Then God made it the stone that holds everything up. In the psalm, the rejected stone is the rescued one, perhaps the king, perhaps Israel itself, despised by the nations and lifted up by God.

‘This is the day’ in verse 24 means the day of this rescue, the day God acted. It is a day for joy.

‘Save us, we pray’ (verse 25) in Hebrew is the cry that comes into English as ‘Hosanna’. At first it was a plea: save us, please. Later it became a shout of praise as well. The Mishnah, written down around AD 200, says that at the Feast of Tabernacles worshippers waved branches when this verse was sung.

The note on Psalm 113 tells how the Hallel was sung at Passover.
passages.later:
When Jesus rode into Jerusalem, the crowds took up this psalm. They cut branches and shouted, “Hosanna to the Son of David!” “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!” (Matthew 21:9). Christians remember this day as Palm Sunday.

A few days later, Jesus quoted verse 22 to the temple leaders who were questioning him: “Have you never read in the Scriptures: ‘The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone’” (Matthew 21:42).

After his resurrection, Peter said the same to the ruling council in Jerusalem, the rulers, elders and scribes with the high priest's family: “This Jesus is ‘the stone you builders rejected, which has become the cornerstone’” (Acts 4:11). The builders there are those particular leaders. It is never a charge against the Jewish people, which this site rejects. Peter wrote later that the stone is “precious” to those who believe (1 Peter 2:7). Paul says the church is built “with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone” (Ephesians 2:20).
passages.asks:
Have you ever been the rejected stone? Psalm 118 says that people's verdict is not the last one. God can take what others threw away and make it the stone that holds the building.

And ‘This is the day’ is not first about every ordinary day. It is about the day God saves. Many Christians read it of the day Jesus rose, since in the psalm it follows the rejected stone made the cornerstone. But once you know that day, you may greet any day with the same words.
